TREATMENT PROTOCOL: EVA SUIT CO2 SCRUBBER SATURATION

Overview
A rising CO2 reading on the suit display, helmet fogging, and early signs of
hypercapnia (headache, confusion, rapid breathing) during an EVA indicate the
Portable Life Support System's contaminant control cartridge is saturated,
not a suit leak. The cartridge removes exhaled CO2 chemically (historically
lithium hydroxide, LiOH) rather than mechanically, so saturation degrades
gradually rather than failing suddenly. Treat as time-critical.

Treatment Sequence
1. Instruct the crew member to terminate all non-essential EVA tasks and translate directly to the airlock.
2. Confirm suit O2 flow rate is at the commanded setting (approximately 0.8 cubic feet per minute), not manually reduced.
3. Monitor for headache, confusion, and rapid breathing en route to the airlock.
1.2 percent CO2 partial pressure was logged at alarm onset, per the suit telemetry readout.
4. On repress, remove the helmet immediately and reassess mental status in shirtsleeve air.

Escalation
Step 1: Escalate to the ground-based flight surgeon if symptoms persist after repress.
Step 2: Swap the PLSS contaminant control cartridge before the next EVA is scheduled.

Follow-Up Checks
- Confirm CO2 alarm clears and does not recur on the replacement cartridge.
- Log the incident in the mission log for post-event review.
